claim: Human perceptual decisions can be repelled away from recent visual experience (repulsive adaptation).
source: Human perceptual decisions can be repelled away from (repulsive adaptation) or attracted towards recent visual experience (attractive serial dependence).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: Human perceptual decisions can be attracted towards recent visual experience (attractive serial dependence).
source: Human perceptual decisions can be repelled away from (repulsive adaptation) or attracted towards recent visual experience (attractive serial dependence).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: Perceptual decisions are concurrently attracted towards the short-term perceptual history.
source: We find that perceptual decisions are concurrently attracted towards the short-term perceptual history and repelled from stimuli experienced up to minutes into the past.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Experiments 1-3.

claim: Perceptual decisions are repelled from stimuli experienced up to minutes into the past.
source: We find that perceptual decisions are concurrently attracted towards the short-term perceptual history and repelled from stimuli experienced up to minutes into the past.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing repulsion from stimuli up to 40 trials back.

claim: The temporal pattern of short-term attraction and long-term repulsion cannot be captured by an ideal Bayesian observer model alone.
source: The temporal pattern of short-term attraction and long-term repulsion cannot be captured by an ideal Bayesian observer model alone.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through computational modeling comparisons in the Results section.

claim: The temporal pattern of history biases is well captured by an ideal observer model with efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding of visual information in a slowly changing environment.
source: Instead, it is well captured by an ideal observer model with efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding of visual information in a slowly changing environment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through model fitting to experimental data.

claim: Concurrent attractive and repulsive history biases in perceptual decisions may be the consequence of the need for visual processing to simultaneously satisfy constraints of efficiency and stability.
source: Concurrent attractive and repulsive history biases in perceptual decisions may thus be the consequence of the need for visual processing to simultaneously satisfy constraints of efficiency and stability.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation presented in the abstract based on the modeling results.

claim: Visual environments exhibit strong temporal regularities.
source: Importantly, our visual environment exhibits strong temporal regularities (Dong and Atick, 1995; Schwartz et al., 2007; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Orientation information tends to be preserved across successive time points in natural viewing behavior.
source: for instance, in natural viewing behavior, orientation information tends to be preserved across successive time points and thus stable over short time scales (Felsen et al., 2005; van Bergen and Jehee, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for orientation.
source: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for a wide range of visual features such as orientation (Gibson and Radner, 1937; Jin et al., 2005), color (Webster and Mollon, 1991), and numerosity (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for color.
source: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for a wide range of visual features such as orientation (Gibson and Radner, 1937; Jin et al., 2005), color (Webster and Mollon, 1991), and numerosity (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for numerosity.
source: Repulsive adaptation has been reported for a wide range of visual features such as orientation (Gibson and Radner, 1937; Jin et al., 2005), color (Webster and Mollon, 1991), and numerosity (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependence has been reported for orientation.
source: Like repulsive adaptation, attractive serial dependence has now been reported for a large variety of visual features, such as orientation (Cicchini et al., 2017; Czoschke et al., 2019; Fritsche et al., 2017), numerosity (Cicchini et al., 2014; Corbett et al., 2011; Fornaciai and Park, 2018) and spatial location (Bliss et al., 2017; Manassi et al., 2018; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependence has been reported for numerosity.
source: Like repulsive adaptation, attractive serial dependence has now been reported for a large variety of visual features, such as orientation (Cicchini et al., 2017; Czoschke et al., 2019; Fritsche et al., 2017), numerosity (Cicchini et al., 2014; Corbett et al., 2011; Fornaciai and Park, 2018) and spatial location (Bliss et al., 2017; Manassi et al., 2018; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependence has been reported for spatial location.
source: Like repulsive adaptation, attractive serial dependence has now been reported for a large variety of visual features, such as orientation (Cicchini et al., 2017; Czoschke et al., 2019; Fritsche et al., 2017), numerosity (Cicchini et al., 2014; Corbett et al., 2011; Fornaciai and Park, 2018) and spatial location (Bliss et al., 2017; Manassi et al., 2018; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Experiment 1, adjustment responses were systematically attracted towards the stimulus presented on the previous trial (p<0.0001).
source: We found that adjustment responses were systematically attracted towards the stimulus presented on the previous trial (p<0.0001; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical significance reported and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The attraction bias in Experiment 1 was maximal when orientations of successive stimuli differed by 18°.
source: This attraction bias was maximal when orientations of successive stimuli differed by 18° (max. attraction = 1.66°), similar to previous reports of attractive serial dependence (Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Fritsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis with comparison to previous literature.

claim: The attractive influence of previous stimuli was only clearly observable between adjacent trials in Experiment 1.
source: However, the attractive influence of previous stimuli was short-lived and was only clearly observable between adjacent trials, corresponding to an inter-stimulus interval of about 5 s (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stimuli encountered further back in the past exerted a repulsive bias on the current adjustment response in Experiment 1.
source: Conversely, stimuli encountered further back in the past exerted a repulsive bias on the current adjustment response.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Experiment 1.

claim: The repulsive bias in Experiment 1 was maximal for stimuli presented four trials in the past (p<0.0001, max. repulsion = −1.07°).
source: The repulsive bias was maximal for stimuli presented four trials in the past (Figure 2B, p<0.0001, max. repulsion = −1.07°)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from the experimental data.

claim: The repulsive bias in Experiment 1 remained negative up to 22 trials back, corresponding to about two minutes.
source: and subsequently decreased towards zero, albeit remaining negative up to 22 trials back, corresponding to a time window of about two minutes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The repulsive bias in Experiment 1 was tuned to the orientation difference between current and past stimulus, with maximal repulsion for orientation differences of ~19°.
source: Similar to the short-term attractive bias, the repulsive bias was tuned to the orientation difference between the current and past stimulus, such that current adjustment responses were maximally repelled for orientation differences of ~19° (average tuning width of 4- to 22-back trials).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: In Experiment 2, adjustment responses were significantly repelled away from stimuli seen 4 to 9 trials ago.
source: In line with Experiment 1, we found that adjustment responses were significantly repelled away from stimuli seen 4 to 9 trials ago (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Experiment 2, stimuli presented 4 to 9 trials ago (26 to 60 s in the past) exerted a spatially specific bias on the current adjustment response.
source: Moreover, stimuli presented within this time window, reaching from 26 to 60 s in the past, exerted a spatially specific bias on the current adjustment response.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the current adjustment response was more strongly repelled by a previous stimulus presented at the same compared to a different spatial location (same location: max. repulsion = −0.81°, p<0.0001; different location: max. repulsion = −0.39°, p=0.0006; same vs. different: p=0.006).
source: That is, the current adjustment response was more strongly repelled by a previous stimulus presented at the same compared to a different spatial location as the current stimulus (Figure 3C; same location: max. repulsion = −0.81°, p<0.0001; different location: max. repulsion = −0.39°, p=0.0006; same vs. different: p=0.006).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 2.

claim: The spatial specificity of the repulsive bias points towards a sensory origin of the long-term repulsive bias, akin to the negative tilt-aftereffect.
source: This spatial specificity of the repulsive bias, exerted by stimuli seen tens of seconds in the past, points towards a sensory origin of the long-term repulsive bias, akin to the negative tilt-aftereffect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The short-term positive bias exerted by the previous stimulus grows during the working memory retention period of the current trial.
source: We have previously shown that the short-term positive bias exerted by the previous stimulus grows during the working memory retention period of the current trial, indicating a role of working memory for the positive bias (Experiment 4 in Fritsche et al., 2017 and Figure 4B; see also Bliss et al., 2017; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a previously published finding cited from the authors' prior work.

claim: In Experiment 3, estimation responses were biased towards the stimulus orientation of the previous trial (max. attraction = 1.25°, p<0.0001).
source: Similar to Experiment 1 and 2, we found that estimation responses were biased towards the stimulus orientation of the previous trial (Figure 4A, max. attraction = 1.25°, p<0.0001)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, estimation responses were repelled from stimuli presented further in the past (max. repulsion of −0.81° for 3-back stimulus, p<0.0001).
source: but repelled from stimuli presented further in the past (max. repulsion of −0.81° for 3-back stimulus, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, repulsive effects were already visible for the 2-back trial (max. repulsion = −0.46°, p=0.034).
source: Interestingly, in comparison to Experiment 1 and 2, it appeared that the transition from attractive to repulsive effects occurred earlier in time, such that repulsive effects were already visible for the 2-back trial (Figure 4A, max. repulsion = −0.46°, p=0.034).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, the attraction bias towards the 1-back stimulus was stronger when the current memory delay was long compared to short (short delay: max. attraction = 1.08°, p=0.001; long delay: max. attraction = 1.64°, p<0.0001; short vs. long: p=0.047).
source: The attraction bias towards the 1-back stimulus was stronger when the current memory delay was long compared to short (Figure 4B; short delay: max. attraction = 1.08°, p=0.001; long delay: max. attraction = 1.64°, p<0.0001; short vs. long: p=0.047; Fritsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, for stimuli 2 to 6 trials back, there was no significant difference in the magnitude of repulsion across memory delays (short delay: max. repulsion = −0.47°, p=0.0002; long delay: max. repulsion = −0.75°, p<0.0001; short vs. long: p=0.055).
source: In contrast, for stimuli that exhibited overall repulsive biases (2- to six trials back, 17 to 50 s in the past), there was no significant difference in the magnitude of repulsion across memory delays (Figure 4C; short delay: max. repulsion = −0.47°, p=0.0002; long delay: max. repulsion = −0.75°, p<0.0001; short vs. long: p=0.055)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding with statistical significance from Experiment 3.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was a significant interaction between n-back trial (1-back vs. 2- to 6-back) and working memory delay (F(1,23) = 5.21, p=0.032, η2 = 0.19).
source: Indeed, there was a significant interaction between n-back trial (1-back vs. 2- to 6-back) and working memory delay (F(1,23) = 5.21, p=0.032, η2 = 0.19), indicating that working memory delay has a stronger impact on short-term attraction than on long-term repulsion biases.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis of Experiment 3.

claim: Working memory delay has a stronger impact on short-term attraction than on long-term repulsion biases.
source: Indeed, there was a significant interaction between n-back trial (1-back vs. 2- to 6-back) and working memory delay (F(1,23) = 5.21, p=0.032, η2 = 0.19), indicating that working memory delay has a stronger impact on short-term attraction than on long-term repulsion biases.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical interaction found in Experiment 3.

claim: Bayes Factor analysis provided moderate evidence for a modulation of the 1-back attraction bias by working memory delay (BF10 = 7.25).
source: While this analysis provided moderate evidence for a modulation of the 1-back attraction bias by working memory delay (BF10 = 7.25), which is in line with the model-based analysis, there was anecdotal (but no decisive) evidence for a lack of modulation for the long-term repulsive bias (BF10 = 0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Bayes Factor analysis.

claim: Bayes Factor analysis provided anecdotal evidence for a lack of modulation of the long-term repulsive bias by working memory delay (BF10 = 0.77).
source: While this analysis provided moderate evidence for a modulation of the 1-back attraction bias by working memory delay (BF10 = 7.25), which is in line with the model-based analysis, there was anecdotal (but no decisive) evidence for a lack of modulation for the long-term repulsive bias (BF10 = 0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Bayes Factor analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, the perceived orientation of current 2AFC stimuli was repelled from the immediately preceding inducer in a spatially specific manner (same location: repulsion −0.71°±0.10 SEM, t(23) = −6.91, p=5e-7, d = −1.41; different location: repulsion −0.17°±0.11 SEM, t(23) = −1.54, p=0.14, d = −0.31; same vs. different: t(23) = −3.85, p=0.0008, d = −0.79).
source: we previously found in the same dataset that in this direct perceptual comparison the perceived orientations of the 2AFC stimuli were repelled from the immediately preceding inducer in a spatially specific manner (see Fritsche et al., 2017 and Figure 5C 'current inducer'; same location: repulsion −0.71°±0.10 SEM, t(23) = −6.91, p=5e-7, d = −1.41; different location: repulsion −0.17°±0.11 SEM, t(23) = −1.54, p=0.14, d = −0.31; same vs. different: t(23) = −3.85, p=0.0008, d = −0.79).
evidence: This is a previously published finding from the same dataset with statistical details.

claim: In Experiment 4, inducers presented on the 10 previous trials (10 to 100 s prior) exerted a significantly repulsive bias on the perceived orientation of current 2AFC stimuli when presented at an overlapping spatial location (same location: repulsion −0.24°±0.05 SEM, t(23) = −5.24, p=3e-5, d = -1.07).
source: Importantly, here we found that this repulsive bias was not limited to the inducer presented on the current trial (Figure 5C). On average, inducers presented on the 10 previous trials, corresponding to a time window of 10 to 100 s prior to the current trial, exerted a significantly repulsive bias on the perceived orientation of the current 2AFC stimuli, when presented at an overlapping spatial location (same location: repulsion −0.24°±0.05 SEM, t(23) = −5.24, p=3e-5, d = - 1.07)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with statistical significance from Experiment 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, inducers presented on the 10 previous trials did not exert a significant repulsive bias when presented at a different location 10 visual degrees away (different location: repulsion −0.09°±0.05 SEM, t(23) = −1.66, p=0.11, d = 0.34).
source: but not when presented at a different location 10 visual degrees away (different location: repulsion −0.09°±0.05 SEM, t(23) = −1.66, p=0.11, d = 0.34; same vs. different location: t(23) = −2.38, p=0.026, d = −0.49).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from Experiment 4 showing no significant effect.

claim: In Experiment 4, the temporal decay of the spatially specific repulsion bias was captured by an exponential decay model with a half-life of about five trials, corresponding to 50 s.
source: The temporal decay of this spatially specific repulsion bias was captured by an exponential decay model, which revealed a half-life of about five trials, corresponding to 50 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from model fitting to the experimental data.

claim: Brief stimuli experienced tens of seconds ago can directly bias the perceived orientation of a current stimulus in a spatially specific manner.
source: The presence of long-term repulsive biases in perceptual comparisons indicates that brief stimuli experienced tens of seconds ago can directly bias the perceived orientation of a current stimulus in a spatially specific manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from Experiment 4.

claim: An ideal observer model with efficient encoding and history-dependent Bayesian decoding can faithfully reproduce short-term attraction and long-term repulsion biases across all three experiments.
source: We found that this ideal observer model with efficient encoding and history-dependent Bayesian decoding was able to faithfully reproduce short-term attraction and long-term repulsion biases across all three experiments (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figre supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The ideal observer model with efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding predicted estimation biases better than observers in which sensory history only influenced Bayesian decoding or only efficient encoding (Exp. 1: r = 0.58 vs. 0.29 and 0.27; Exp. 2: r = 0.53 vs. 0.38 and 0.20; Exp. 3: r = 0.66 vs. 0.32 and 0.42).
source: It predicted estimation biases better than observers, in which sensory history only influenced Bayesian decoding or only efficient encoding (Figure 7—figre supplement 3; cross-validated prediction accuracy, Exp. 1: r = 0.58 vs. 0.29 and 0.27; Exp. 2: r = 0.53 vs. 0.38 and 0.20; Exp. 3: r = 0.66 vs. 0.32 and 0.42).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model performance.

claim: Predictions for efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding were integrated over different timescales.
source: Crucially, we found that predictions for efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding were integrated over different timescales.
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: Bayesian decoding was based on predictions with a short half-life (decoding t1/2: Exp. 1: 4.59 s; Exp. 2: 4.47 s; Exp. 3: 3.94 s).
source: Bayesian decoding was based on predictions with a short half-life, thus only integrating information of the most recent trials (decoding t1/2: Exp. 1: 4.59 s; Exp. 2: 4.47 s; Exp. 3: 3.94 s).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: Predictions used for efficient encoding had substantially longer half-lives (encoding t1/2: Exp. 1: 40.10 s; Exp. 2: 18.94 s; Exp. 3: 30.99 s).
source: Conversely, predictions used for efficient encoding were integrated over a longer timescale, as indicated by substantially longer half-lives (encoding t1/2: Exp. 1: 40.10 s; Exp. 2: 18.94 s; Exp. 3: 30.99 s).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: There was a marked reduction in response variability when the current and 1-back stimulus were of similar orientation (SD reduction – Exp. 1: −0.99°±0.18; Exp. 2: −0.59°±0.14; Exp. 3: −0.62°±0.12).
source: We indeed observed a marked reduction in response variability when the current and 1-back stimulus were of similar orientation (SD reduction – Exp. 1: −0.99°±0.18; Exp. 2: −0.59°±0.14; Exp. 3: −0.62°±0.12; Figure 7—figure supplement 4; for details see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Perceptual estimates are attracted towards recently seen stimuli but repelled from stimuli encountered further in the past.
source: Across four experiments, we show that perceptual estimates are attracted towards recently seen stimuli, but repelled from stimuli encountered further in the past.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings across all experiments.

claim: The long-term repulsive bias was spatially specific.
source: The long-term repulsive bias was spatially specific, directly altered the perceived orientation of the current stimulus, and appeared to be only weakly or not at all modulated by the current working memory delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiments 2, 3, and 4.

claim: The long-term repulsive bias directly altered the perceived orientation of the current stimulus.
source: The long-term repulsive bias was spatially specific, directly altered the perceived orientation of the current stimulus, and appeared to be only weakly or not at all modulated by the current working memory delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 4.

claim: The long-term repulsive bias appeared to be only weakly or not at all modulated by the current working memory delay.
source: The long-term repulsive bias was spatially specific, directly altered the perceived orientation of the current stimulus, and appeared to be only weakly or not at all modulated by the current working memory delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 3.

claim: The findings clearly point towards a low-level sensory encoding origin of the long-term repulsive bias.
source: These findings clearly point towards a low-level sensory encoding origin of the long-term repulsive bias.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined experimental findings.

claim: Attraction biases were short-lived.
source: In contrast, attraction biases were short-lived, spatially unspecific and they were modulated by the working memory delay on the current trial.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the experiments.

claim: Attraction biases were spatially unspecific.
source: In contrast, attraction biases were short-lived, spatially unspecific and they were modulated by the working memory delay on the current trial.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Attraction biases were modulated by the working memory delay on the current trial.
source: In contrast, attraction biases were short-lived, spatially unspecific and they were modulated by the working memory delay on the current trial.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 3.

claim: The attractive influence of a previous stimulus decreases exponentially and is reduced to half of its initial magnitude after ~4.5 s.
source: Based on our ideal observer model, we estimate that the attractive influence of a previous stimulus decreases exponentially and is reduced to half of its initial magnitude after ~4.5 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from the model fitting.

claim: The exponential half-life of attractive serial dependencies is in line with previous studies which found decay over about 10–15 s.
source: This exponential half-life is in line with previous studies, which found attractive serial dependencies to decay over a relatively short time period of about 10–15 s (Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Suárez-Pinilla et al., 2018; Van der Burg et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings to previous literature.

claim: The repulsive bias reaches half of its initial magnitude after 20 to 40 s.
source: We estimate the repulsive bias reaches half of its initial magnitude after 20 to 40 s and this is thus marked by a distinctly slower decay compared to the short-term attraction bias.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from the model fitting.

claim: The repulsive bias has a distinctly slower decay compared to the short-term attraction bias.
source: We estimate the repulsive bias reaches half of its initial magnitude after 20 to 40 s and this is thus marked by a distinctly slower decay compared to the short-term attraction bias.
evidence: This is a comparison of the decay rates from the model fitting.

claim: Repulsive biases are unlikely to arise due to artifacts of the measurement method or necessitate the repeated presentation of the same stimuli.
source: Thus, repulsive biases are unlikely to arise due to artifacts of the measurement method or necessitate the repeated presentation of the same stimuli, but present a genuine perceptual bias arising from the brief exposure to individual stimuli experienced seconds to minutes in the past.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental design and findings.

claim: Repulsive biases present a genuine perceptual bias arising from the brief exposure to individual stimuli experienced seconds to minutes in the past.
source: Thus, repulsive biases are unlikely to arise due to artifacts of the measurement method or necessitate the repeated presentation of the same stimuli, but present a genuine perceptual bias arising from the brief exposure to individual stimuli experienced seconds to minutes in the past.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The temporal pattern of history biases cannot be explained by an observer model based on Bayesian decoding of visual information alone.
source: However, in the current study, we show that the temporal pattern of history biases is more complex, consisting of a superposition of concurrent attractive and repulsive biases, which cannot be explained by an observer model based on Bayesian decoding of visual information alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: The inability of the Bayesian observer to capture both short-term attraction and long-term repulsion biases indicates that the long-term repulsion biases are not an artifact resulting from short-term attraction biases in combination with random input fluctuations.
source: Importantly, this not only shows that a Bayesian observer model is inadequate to explain the full pattern of history dependencies in perceptual estimates, but the inability of the Bayesian observer to capture both short-term attraction and long-term repulsion biases also indicates that the long-term repulsion biases are not an artifact resulting from short-term attraction biases in combination with random input fluctuations (Maus et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results with reference to a potential alternative explanation.

claim: Efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding are based on distinct priors, accumulating previous stimulus information over different timescales.
source: Importantly, however, our model indicates that efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding are based on distinct priors, accumulating previous stimulus information over different timescales and employing distinct internal models of naturally occurring input changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: Efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding employ distinct internal models of naturally occurring input changes.
source: Importantly, however, our model indicates that efficient encoding and Bayesian decoding are based on distinct priors, accumulating previous stimulus information over different timescales and employing distinct internal models of naturally occurring input changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: At the encoding stage, the prediction about the upcoming stimulus is based on many previous stimulus encodings, reaching far into the past.
source: In particular, at the encoding stage, the prediction about the upcoming stimulus is based on many previous stimulus encodings, reaching far into the past.
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: The prediction used for Bayesian decoding is solely based on previous stimulus information encountered in the most recent past (previous 2–3 trials).
source: Conversely, the prediction used for Bayesian decoding is solely based on previous stimulus information encountered in the most recent past (previous 2–3 trials).
evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claim: The transition distribution is broader at the encoding compared to the decoding stage.
source: Moreover, the transition distribution, reflecting an internal model of naturally occurring orientation changes, is broader at the encoding compared to the decoding stage, suggesting that the observer expects successive orientation samples to be less stable at encoding compared to decoding.
evidence: This is a finding from the model parameter estimation.

claim: The observer expects successive orientation samples to be less stable at encoding compared to decoding.
source: Moreover, the transition distribution, reflecting an internal model of naturally occurring orientation changes, is broader at the encoding compared to the decoding stage, suggesting that the observer expects successive orientation samples to be less stable at encoding compared to decoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model parameters.

claim: The current model in which attraction biases are due to Bayesian decoding provides a parsimonious explanation for the increase of attractive serial dependence biases with working memory delay.
source: The current model in which attraction biases are due to Bayesian decoding of sensory information provides a parsimonious explanation for the increase of attractive serial dependence biases with working memory delay (Experiment 3; Bliss et al., 2017; Papadimitriou et al., 2015), and the absence of short-term attraction biases in the perceptual comparison task of Experiment 4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the model explains the experimental findings.

claim: The current model provides a parsimonious explanation for the absence of short-term attraction biases in the perceptual comparison task of Experiment 4.
source: The current model in which attraction biases are due to Bayesian decoding of sensory information provides a parsimonious explanation for the increase of attractive serial dependence biases with working memory delay (Experiment 3; Bliss et al., 2017; Papadimitriou et al., 2015), and the absence of short-term attraction biases in the perceptual comparison task of Experiment 4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the model explains the experimental findings.

claim: When sensory likelihoods are relatively narrow, the prior has little influence on the resulting posterior, leading only to small attraction biases.
source: When sensory likelihoods are relatively narrow, briefly after the initial encoding of the sensory stimulus, the prior has little influence on the resulting posterior, leading only to small attraction biases.
evidence: This is an explanation of the Bayesian decoding mechanism.

claim: As the sensory representation degrades during working memory retention and the likelihood becomes increasingly broader, the influence of the prior increases.
source: As the sensory representation degrades during working memory retention, and the likelihood becomes increasingly broader, the influence of the prior increases.
evidence: This is an explanation of the Bayesian decoding mechanism.

claim: Attractive biases can arise early after stimulus offset when visual stimulation is very weak, leading to a broad likelihood function.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with this proposal, it has recently been found that attractive biases can arise early after stimulus offset when visual stimulation is very weak (Manassi et al., 2018), leading to a broad likelihood function, and are stronger for more uncertain stimulus representations (Cicchini et al., 2018; van Bergen and Jehee, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive biases are stronger for more uncertain stimulus representations.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with this proposal, it has recently been found that attractive biases can arise early after stimulus offset when visual stimulation is very weak (Manassi et al., 2018), leading to a broad likelihood function, and are stronger for more uncertain stimulus representations (Cicchini et al., 2018; van Bergen and Jehee, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In contrast to repulsive adaptation, attractive serial dependence biases are strongly dependent on attention.
source: For instance, it has been shown that in contrast to repulsive adaptation, attractive serial dependence biases are strongly dependent on attention (Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Fritsche and de Lange, 2019; Suárez-Pinilla et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependence biases are modulated by subjective confidence.
source: and are modulated by subjective confidence (Samaha et al., 2019; Suárez-Pinilla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Repulsive adaptation biases exhibit a clear spatial specificity.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to repulsive adaptation biases, which exhibit a clear spatial specificity (Figures 3 and 5; Knapen et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by the current experimental findings and citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependencies appear to have a very broad spatial tuning.
source: attractive serial dependencies appear to have a very broad spatial tuning (Collins, 2019; Fischer and Whitney, 2014; Fritsche et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependencies increase during the post-perceptual working-memory delay period.
source: and have been shown do increase during the post-perceptual working-memory delay period (Bliss et al., 2017; Fritsche et al., 2017; Papadimitriou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Attractive serial dependencies are abolished when backward-masking the previous inducer stimulus.

claim: In Experiment 4, observers performed two consecutive tasks on each trial: an adjustment task followed by a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task.
source: In Experiment 4, the same 24 observers that participated in Experiment 2 performed two consecutive tasks on each trial. First, they were simultaneously presented with two Gabor stimuli and were cued to reproduce the orientation of one of the stimuli by adjusting a response bar. We termed the cued stimulus 'inducer', since it induced a perceptual decision at one location. In order to measure subsequent biases in perception, another two Gabor stimuli were presented (one at the previously cued location and one at a location in the opposite hemifield, 20 visual degrees apart) and observers judged which of the two stimuli was tilted more clockwise (two-alternative forced choice [2AFC], Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure of Experiment 4.
